docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. It is a security mechanism designed to distinguish between human users and automated bots on the internet.

docs.title: Why CAPTCHA Exists
docs.text:
• Websites are constantly targeted by automated programs (bots) that:
  • Create fake accounts
  • Send spam messages
  • Scrape data
  • Perform brute-force attacks
  • To protect against these threats, CAPTCHAs provide small tests that are easy for humans but hard for machines.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
• Automated generation and grading: The system must be able to automatically create the challenge and verify the solution.
  • Asymmetry: The task should be solvable by a human with minimal effort, but require significant resources for a bot.
  • Accessibility considerations: CAPTCHAs must remain usable for people with disabilities (e.g., offering audio alternatives).

Next: We’ll explore the History of CAPTCHA, from its invention in the early 2000s to modern reCAPTCHA.

docs.title: Origins (Late 1990s – Early 2000s)
docs.text:
The concept of CAPTCHA was introduced in the early 2000s by Luis von Ahn, Manuel Blum, Nicholas Hopper, and John Langford at Carnegie Mellon University. They developed the first CAPTCHA system to prevent bots from abusing online services, such as free email providers (e.g., Yahoo, Hotmail).

  • 2000: The term CAPTCHA was coined.
  • The first CAPTCHAs were text-based distorted characters, designed to be human-readable but difficult for computer programs.

docs.title: Growth and Adoption (2000s)
docs.text:
As bots became more sophisticated, CAPTCHAs started appearing across: - Email providers – to prevent automated sign-ups. - E-commerce sites – to stop ticket scalping and fake purchases. - Forums and blogs – to reduce spam.

During this period: - Text CAPTCHAs became widespread. - Spammers began creating optical character recognition (OCR) programs to break weak CAPTCHAs. - Some companies paid human workers (captcha farms) to solve challenges in bulk.

docs.title: reCAPTCHA (2007 – Present)
docs.text:
In 2007, Luis von Ahn and his team launched reCAPTCHA, a project that combined security with a social good:

  • Instead of random characters, reCAPTCHA used scanned words from old books and newspapers that OCR programs couldn’t recognize.
  • When millions of people solved CAPTCHAs daily, they were unknowingly helping digitize books and preserve cultural heritage.

docs.title: Acquisition by Google (2009)
docs.text: Google acquired reCAPTCHA in 2009. This marked a new era: - Improved security through image-based challenges (select all traffic lights, crosswalks, etc.). - Integration into Google services and millions of websites. - reCAPTCHA became the standard for bot protection.

docs.title: Modern reCAPTCHA (2014 – Today)
docs.text:
Google released multiple new versions:

  • reCAPTCHA v2 (2014):
  • The famous “I am not a robot” checkbox.

  • If suspicious, users solve image puzzles (traffic lights, buses, etc.).

  • Invisible reCAPTCHA (2017):

  • No user interaction needed unless activity looks suspicious.

  • Runs silently in the background.

  • reCAPTCHA v3 (2018):

  • No challenges at all.
  • Uses behavioral analysis (mouse movements, clicks, browsing patterns) to assign a “human score.”
  • Site owners decide how to act on suspicious users.

docs.title: Today
docs.text:
CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA are used on millions of websites globally. They remain a critical defense mechanism against automated abuse, though challenges exist in usability and accessibility.
